title: Effect of intercritical annealing time and processing route on the tensile and shear mechanical properties of dual-phase (DP) steel
abstract:
Dual-phase (DP) steels were processed through the intercritical annealing (IA) and intermediate quenching (IQ) routes, where the holding time in the two-phase region was the main processing parameter. It was revealed that the insufficient holding time leads to an incomplete phase transformation with lower martensite volume fractions (V
                     m); while excessive holding time causes grain coarsening in the IA route and abnormal grain growth (AGG) in the IQ method. On the other hand, for the optimum holding time, the IQ route led to a finer ferrite grain size and the refinement of the martensite island size (S
                     m) with a uniform dispersion, leading to a superior strength-ductility synergy due to the improved work-hardening rate (θ) according to θ∝√(V
                     m/S
                     m). However, unnecessarily long holding time in the IQ route triggered AGG and significantly impaired the mechanical properties. In addition, shear punch testing (SPT) was used to evaluate the shear mechanical properties, with trends similar to those observed in the tensile deformation mode. Moreover, the tensile and shear properties were successfully correlated according to the plasticity theory. In summary, this work emphasized the importance of the processing route and close control of the intercritical annealing time for the improvement of microstructure and mechanical properties of DP steels as the flagship of advanced high-strength steels (AHSSs).
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High strength combined with desirable ductility and low production costs are among the outstanding properties of dual-phase (DP) steels, which have led to their widespread applications, particularly in the automotive industry [ 1–3 ]. These steels have microstructures consisting of a ferritic matrix and a martensite phase as a secondary phase (10–30 vol%). The soft ferritic matrix increases elongation and ductility, while the hard martensite islands help to increase the strength of the material [ 4–6 ]. To achieve a dual-phase microstructure in low-carbon steels, the intercritical annealing followed by water quenching is usually employed. This treatment, which can be applied based on different routes, would affect the microstructure and mechanical properties [ 7 , 8 ]. In this regard, the intercritical annealing (IA) of ferritic-pearlitic microstructure [ 8 , 9 ] and intermediate quenching (IQ) via intercritical annealing of a martensitic microstructure [ 10–12 ] are among the most-widely used ones. The mechanical behavior of dual-phase steels is controlled by several factors, including ferrite grain size [ 13–15 ], martensite volume fraction [ 16–18 ], and martensite morphology and its carbon content [ 19–21 ]. It is possible to tailor these microstructural parameters through different processing routes, including IA and IQ routes, to achieve specific mechanical properties in DP steels.

Besides the intercritical annealing temperature, the intercritical annealing time is also quite important for the development of the DP microstructure [ 22 , 23 ]. It should be long enough to obtain the desired volume fraction of austenite, which transforms to martensite upon quenching [ 24 , 25 ]. However, long holding times might lead to the coarsening of the microstructure and deterioration of mechanical properties [ 26 , 27 ]. Since the mechanism of microstructural evolution during IA differs for different initial microstructures, the response of the IA and IQ routes to the intercritical annealing time is different, which needs to be evaluated for the DP steels with specific chemical compositions.

While the tensile properties of DP steels have been widely studied, the shear properties have received less attention. In this regard, the shear punch testing (SPT) as a miniature testing method has widely been used to evaluate the mechanical properties [ 28 , 29 ], creep and superplasticity [ 30 , 31 ], and stress corrosion cracking [ 32 , 33 ]. Moreover, significant efforts have been made to correlate shear punch test results with those from uniaxial tensile tests [ 34–37 ]. Regarding the shear punch testing of DP steels, there are a few reports [ 38–40 ]. Qu et al. [ 38 ] investigated the mechanical properties of a 0.07C-1.84Mn-0.09Si DP steel by SPT, where the intercritical annealing temperatures of 750 and 800 °C and the holding time of 2 min was used to change the martensite volume fraction. They reported an increase in the maximum force by increasing the intercritical annealing temperature. In another investigation, Qu et al. [ 39 ] also evaluated the dynamic deformation behavior of DP steel. Moreover, Sellamuthu [ 34 ] studied the correlation between tensile and shear properties for a specific DP steel (DP590) and other alloys.

Therefore, the evaluation of the shear properties of DP steels using SPT and characterizing the effects of processing route and intercritical annealing time remained as a research gap, which needs more investigation. Moreover, the relationship between the tensile and shear properties of DP steel and evaluating the effect of processing history needs to be unraveled. Accordingly, the present work aims to investigate these subjects.

sections.heading: Material and processing
paragraphs:
In this research, cold-rolled St37 sheets with chemical composition of 0.2C-0.37Mn-0.23Si (wt.%) and a thickness of 1 mm was used to process dual-phase steel. The critical temperatures were determined using the JMatPro software and Trzaska equations, which are among the widely used methods for estimating phase transformation temperatures in steels. The Trzaska equations are presented below [ 40 ]: 
                            
                               (1) 
                               
                                  A c 1  = 742–29C – 14Mn + 13Si + 16Cr – 17Ni – 16Mo + 45V + 36Cu 
                            
                         
                         
                            
                               (2) 
                               
                                  A c 3  = 925–219√C – 7Mn + 39Si – 16Ni + 13Mo + 97V

The JMatPro software [ 41 ] predicted Ac 1  and Ac 3  temperatures of 729 °C and 835 °C, respectively; whereas the respective temperatures determined via the Treska equations were 734 °C and 833 °C. It can be seen that the predictions of both methods are consistent. Accordingly, the JMatPro predicted temperatures were considered in this work. As shown in  Fig. 1 
                         a and b, two heat treatment routes of IA and IQ were used to achieve the dual-phase ferrite-martensite microstructures. To investigate the effect of holding time in the intercritical regime, the sheets were intercritically annealed at 760 °C for 1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min and then quenched in water. It was performed in a standard muffle furnace without protective atmosphere. Although slight surface oxidation occurred for longer holding times, the affected surface layer was completely removed by grinding and polishing prior to all microstructural observations and mechanical tests. Therefore, oxidation has not influenced the results discussed in this work.

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: For microstructural characterization, the sheets were first ground using a series of SiC abrasive papers, followed by polishing with a soft cloth to achieve a high quality surface finish suitable for optical and electron microscopy. After etching with a 2 % Nital solution, microstructural analysis was performed using both a Leitz optical microscope and a MIRA3 TESCAN field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM). The volume fraction of martensite was assessed via image analysis technique. Using a PHILIPS PW-3710 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation, the dislocation density of samples were calculated based on the Williamson-Hall method [ 42 , 43 ].

sections.heading: Characterization of mechanical behavior
paragraphs: The mechanical properties of the DP steels were evaluated using tensile testing and SPT at room temperature in an MTS machine. Both the tensile test and the SPT were performed at an equivalent strain rate of 1.7 × 10 −3  s −1 . The tensile test specimens were prepared according to the subsize ASTM  E8  standard with a gauge length of 25 mm, as shown in  Fig. 1 c. The SPT setup included a flat-ended punch with a diameter of 3.044 mm and a die with a diameter of 3.144 mm, as shown in  Fig. 1 d [ 44 ]. For SPT, the samples were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 1 mm sections and then ground using SiC abrasive paper to a final thickness of 0.7 mm. Vickers hardness tests were performed using a load of 5 kgf with a dwell time of 30 s.

sections.heading: Microstructural evaluations
paragraphs:
Optical micrographs of DP steels obtained by IA route are depicted in  Fig. 2 
                         a to f. In the IA route, the formation of the dual-phase microstructure begins with the transformation of pearlite into austenite, followed by the nucleation and growth of austenite at the ferrite grain boundaries. After quenching, the austenite transformed into martensite, forming a dual-phase ferrite-martensitic structure [ 45 , 46 ].

As can be seen in  Fig. 2 b, IA of 1 min was not enough to completely transform pearlite into austenite and some pearlitic colonies remain in the structure after quenching. Therefore, a triplex microstructure consisting of ferrite + pearlite + martensite was formed, where martensite phase is marked with red arrows and pearlite with blue ones ( Fig. 2 b). However, increasing the intercritical annealing time to 5 min resulted in the formation of a DP microstructure with increased martensite volume fraction ( V 
                         m ), as shown in  Fig. 2 c. Further increase in the intercritical annealing time did not change the  V 
                         m ; while it had a significant effect on the ferrite grain size. As shown in  Fig. 2 g, the average grain size of the ferrite ( D 
                         f ) increased from 25.4 ± 2.1 to 50.9 ± 3.4 μm as the intercritical annealing time was extended from 5 to 120 min. This grain coarsening might have a substantial impact on the overall mechanical behavior of the DP steel [ 47–49 ]. For summarization, the effects of intercritical annealing time on the  D 
                         f ,  V 
                         m , and the measured hardness are shown in  Fig. 2 h. It can be seen that  V 
                         m  increases with annealing time, reaching 30.1 % at 5 min. Beyond this point, the martensite content remains essentially constant up to 120 min of annealing. The hardness follows a similar trend, initially increasing due to the strengthening effect of the martensite as the secondary phase [ 16–18 ], and reaching a maximum of 217  H 
                         V  for the sample annealed for 5 min. However, with extended annealing time, hardness begins to decrease due to the coarsening of ferrite grains (increasing  D 
                         f ).

The microstructural evolution of DP steels processed via the IQ route is presented in  Fig. 3 
                         a to g. The results reveal that the IQ route produces a finer microstructure compared to the IA route ( Fig. 2 ). In this process, the martensitic structure is intercritically annealed, providing numerous nucleation sites for both austenite and ferrite formation. This enhanced nucleation activity contributes to a more refined and uniformly distributed microstructure at an optimum intercritical annealing time [ 24–27 ]. These aspects can be further evaluated based on the FESEM analysis.  Fig. 4 
                          presents the FESEM images, illustrating the initial structures and the microstructure evolutions occurring during the IA and IQ heat treatment processes.  Fig. 4 a displays the normalized pearlite-ferrite structure; while  Fig. 4 b clearly reveals the IA1 triplex structure that previously discussed.  Fig. 4 c presents the microstructure of the IA5 sample, which is predominantly composed of ferrite and martensite. The increased martensite fraction suggests a higher intercritical annealing time, resulting in more austenite formation and subsequent transformation upon cooling.  Fig. 4 d to e depict the initial martensitic structure and the dual-phase microstructures produced by the IQ method, which exhibit a finer grain size and a more homogeneous distribution of martensite islands within the ferrite matrix compared to IA method.

As can be deduced from  Fig. 3 , the abnormal grain growth (AGG) of the ferritic matrix occurs with increasing holding time, which is characterized by a mixture of small grains alongside larger ferrite grains. It has been reported that the IQ route or low prior deformation might lead to the emergence of AGG during IA [ 50–52 ].  Fig. 3 h illustrates the variations in average grain size and its distribution for different intercritical annealing times. With IA of the martensitic structure from 1 to 15 min, the  V 
                         m  increases and reaches its maximum value; while the average grain size increases from 7.4 ± 0.6 to 15.8 ± 1.3 μm with a relatively uniform distribution. However, at longer annealing times, this uniformity diminishes as AGG becomes more pronounced, particularly at an annealing duration of 120 min.

As depicted in  Fig. 3 i, in the IQ route, it takes 15 min to reach the maximum  V 
                         m , after which it remains constant. The maximum hardness achieved in this process is 307  H 
                         V  at the holding time of 15 min, which is significantly higher compared with the maximum hardness obtained in the IA method (217  H 
                         V ). This increase in hardness is attributed to the finer grain structure [ 27 , 53 ] and possibly the higher dislocation density in the IQ-treated samples. In this regard, the XRD patterns of  Fig. 5 
                         a were used to obtain the dislocation densities reported in  Fig. 5 b. It can be observed that the normalized sample shows a low dislocation density; while the fully martensitic sample exhibits a high dislocation density. However, the IA5 and IQ15 DP steels show nearly similar dislocation densities. Accordingly, the dislocation density of the samples depends on the martensite content. Therefore, the main reason for the increased hardness of the IQ15 sample compared to the IA5 sample is the finer microstructure of the IQ15 sample, as will be revisited later based on the work-hardening rate plots.

As discussed above, extending the holding time beyond 15 min leads to the occurrence of abnormal grain growth, which negatively impacts mechanical properties, including hardness. This deterioration is clearly seen in  Fig. 3 i, where the effect of grain coarsening on hardness reduction becomes apparent.

sections.heading: Tensile mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Based on the observed trends in hardness and microstructural analysis in  Figs. 2 and 3 , some representative samples that exhibited the most notable changes were considered for further analysis. The purpose of this selective approach was to focus on samples that best reflect the influence of the heat treatment on the mechanical properties, while avoiding redundant testing of conditions showing similar behavior. Accordingly, the engineering stress-strain curves obtained from the tensile tests of selected samples are shown in  Fig. 6 
                         a and b for the IA and IQ routes, respectively. The yield point phenomenon can be observed in the tensile curve of the normalized sample, as shown in  Fig. 6 a. This effect can be attributed to the presence of Cottrell atmospheres, where interstitial atoms such as carbon pin dislocations [ 54 , 55 ]. This phenomenon became less pronounced after intercritical annealing time of 1 min. This is related to the austenite formation during IA, which transforms to martensite upon cooling to room temperature and provides some free dislocations in ferrite around the martensite islands [ 13 , 55 , 56 ]. With a longer holding time, the pearlite is completely dissolved and the yield point phenomenon is completely eliminated, as can be seen in the tensile curve of the sample annealed for 5 min. In contrast, the stress-strain curves of all IQ-treated samples show continuous yielding behavior with no evidence of a yield point phenomenon, as depicted in  Fig. 6 b. This suggests that the microstructural evolution in the IQ route leads to a more homogeneous phase distribution, preventing the formation of localized dislocation pinning sites and ensuring a smoother transition from elastic to plastic deformation.

For the IA-treated samples ( Fig. 6 a), the tensile yield strength (TYS) and the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) reach the maximum value for the intercritical annealing time of 5 min, which corresponds to the first instance of the attainment of the maximum  V 
                         m  with relatively fine ferrite grain size. This also coincides with the decrease in the total elongation, as a consequence of the well-known strength-ductility trade-off [ 57–60 ]. By further increasing the intercritical annealing time, as the  V 
                         m  remains constant but the  D 
                         f  increases ( Fig. 2 h), the TYS and UTS decrease. For the IQ-treated samples ( Fig. 6 b), IA for 1 min resulted in a pronounced drop of the TYS and UTS but significant increase in ductility, when compared to the initial martensitic sample. Then, upon increasing the intercritical annealing time to 15 min, the TYS and UTS increase, because of the increase in  V 
                         m . However, longer annealing times (such as 120 min) impair the mechanical properties due to the emergence of the AGG ( Fig. 3 ).

An important observation is the superior mechanical properties of the IQ-treated samples compared to the IA-treated ones. The maximum UTS in the IQ route is 992 MPa for the sample annealed for 15 min (IQ15); while in the IA method, the highest UTS is 693 MPa for the holding time of 5 min (IA5). More importantly, the improvement in strength has been achieved without compromising the ductility, as both samples show a total elongation of ∼16.6 %, which further highlights the benefits of the IQ processing method in improving mechanical performance of DP steels.  Fig. 6 c illustrates the strength–ductility balance of advanced steels [ 61 ] along with the findings of the current research. As demonstrated, most of the DP steel samples investigated in this work fall within the typical range for DP steels (marked by the black hatched area). However, the IQ15 sample demonstrates superior mechanical performance compared to the other DP samples and exhibits an excellent strength–ductility balance, approaching the product of strength and ductility of 20 GPa%. On the other hand, a large drop in the strength-ductility balance can be seen for the IQ120 sample.

Fig. 7 
                         a compares the work-hardening behaviors of the normalized, IA5, and IQ15 samples. Comparing the normalized sample with the DP samples reveals the importance of the disappearance of the yield-point phenomenon in the work-hardening behavior of the DP samples at the beginning of plastic deformation. Moreover, the levels of the work-hardening rate ( θ ) in the DP samples in the plastic range are significantly higher. A comparison of the IA5 and IQ15 samples shows a significant enhancement in work-hardening characteristics in the latter. Notably, in the IQ15 sample, the intersection of the true stress and  θ  takes place at higher strain values, indicating an increase in uniform elongation and the work-hardening exponent ( n ) according to the Considère criterion [ 3 , 62–64 ]. The  n -vale for the IA5 and IQ15 samples was determined as 0.11 and 0.13, respectively.

The microstructural refinement of DP steels in terms of the refinement of ferrite grains [ 65–68 ] and the martensite islands contribute to the increase in  θ  [ 69–71 ]. It has been shown that  θ  in DP steels is directly affected by the ratio of √( V 
                         m / S 
                         m ), where  S 
                         m  refers to the average size of martensite islands [ 70 , 71 ]. In the case of the IQ15 and IA5 samples, with a similar  V 
                         m  (∼30 vol%),  θ  level of the IQ15 is higher, which is related to the fact that the  S 
                         m  decreased from ∼12.8 ± 4.8 μm for IA5 sample to 6.7 ± 1.6 μm for the IQ15 sample, as clearly shown in  Fig. 7 b. This trend correlates well with the previous discussion comparing these samples, further reinforcing the relationship between microstructural refinement and improved work hardening behavior. These results emphasize the crucial influence of martensite morphology on regulating strain-hardening characteristics, underscoring the importance of microstructural tailoring through optimized heat treatment processes.

sections.heading: Shear mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The shear punch curves of different samples are shown in  Fig. 9 
                         a and b. Moreover, the obtained values of the shear yield stress (SYS) and ultimate shear strength (USS) are summarized in  Fig. 9 c, where the USS values range between 278 and 394 MPa for the IA-treated samples and between 349 and 579 MPa for the IQ-treated ones. This reveals the superiority of IQ samples and a similar trend compared to the tensile properties can be seen.

Fig. 9 d demonstrate the dependency of SYS and USS with TYS and UTS for both the IA and IQ groups and indicates that the SYS/TYS values are in agreement with the theoretical line anticipated by the von-Mises criterion (2 σ 
                         2  = 6 τ 
                         2 , where  σ  is the tensile stress and  τ  is the shear stress) [ 62 ], as marked with a black dashed line in  Fig. 9 d. Nonetheless, while the USS/UTS values show a good agreement with the von-Mises line, a minor deviation from the theoretical correlation is observable. This deviation can be related to the differences in work-hardening behaviors during tensile and shear tests.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The effect of intercritical annealing time and processing route on the tensile and shear mechanical properties of DP steel, based on the St37 sheets, were investigated. The following conclusions can be drawn from this work. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            It was revealed that an insufficient holding time in the IA range leads to incomplete phase transformation, the retention of some pearlite colonies the microstructure, and lower martensite content, which cannot eliminate the yield-point phenomenon at the start of plastic deformation. This microstructure is not favorable for the improvements in the mechanical properties and work-hardening behavior. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            For the optimum holding time of 5 min at 760 °C, the IA route (IA5 sample) led to a fine  D 
                               f  of 25.4 ± 2.1 μm and  S 
                               m  of 12.8 ± 4.8 μm. However, for the optimum holding time of 15 min at 760 °C, the IQ route (IQ15 sample) led to a fine  D 
                               f  of 15.8 ± 1.3 μm and  S 
                               m  of 6.7 ± 1.6 μm with uniform dispersion. The finer microstructure of the IQ15 sample led to a superior strength-ductility synergy due to the improved  θ  according to  θ ∝√( V 
                               m / S 
                               m ), with TYS, UTS, and total elongation of 491 MPa, 992 MPa, and 16.6 %, respectively. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The unnecessary long holding times in the IA range resulted in grain coarsening in the IA route and triggered AGG in the IQ method, with the  V 
                               m  remaining at the equilibrium content. This significantly impaired the mechanical properties. For instance, the IQ120 sample had TYS, UTS, and total elongation of 316 MPa, 597 MPa, and 13.1 %, respectively. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            Calculated UTS values, predicted using the known correlation between hardness and tensile strength, were in agreement with the experimentally obtained values. Moreover, SPT was also used to evaluate the shear mechanical properties, leading to similar trends seen for the tensile testing. Furthermore, the tensile and shear properties were successfully correlated according to the von-Mises criterion, which makes it possible to estimate the tensile and shear properties from the other one.
